Reporting requirements for ‘batch matching’ Within the SIDC, an increase in cross-border capacity may lead to the coupling of two order books. In such cases, compatible orders initially placed on the individual order books are automatically matched by the trading system via a different matching process (batch matching), which is referred as ‘mini-auctions’. With reference to the reporting of mini-auctions, it is ACER’s understanding that the orders maintain the same order ID and are automatically transferred without any action by the market participants to the mini-auction, lasting a few seconds. Such a mini-auction represents a technical solution for the auto-matching system of the orders in the intraday coupling algorithm, but from the data reporting point of view there is no need to report such an event by suspending the continuous session and reporting the orders in the mini-auction with a different contract ID. In such cases it is necessary to flag the trades resulting from such an auto-matching functionality of the intraday coupling algorithm by populating Data field (43) Transaction type with ‘BM’ for ‘batch matching’. Lifecycle reporting requirements General reporting requirements for the reporting of lifecycle events of transactions traded on continuous markets shall apply. For further information, see Annex I to the TRUM.

units.b: Day-ahead auctions within single day-ahead coupling
units.t: The Single Day-Ahead Coupling (SDAC) is a pan-European electricity market mechanism connecting the national day-ahead electricity markets into a coordinated auction through a common algorithm. Reporting requirements for on the contract ID and contract name Like the reporting requirements provided for transactions placed and concluded within the SIDC, in the case of day-ahead auctions involved in market coupling, both Data Field (23) Contract ID and Data Field (24) Contract name shall start with the prefix ‘SDAC_’. In the case of Data Field (23), the prefix shall be followed by the contract ID code assigned at the centralised level by SDAC. Transaction timestamp In ACER’s view, the transactions timestamp for trades in the case of SDAC shall reflect the time of publication of the global preliminary solution (GlobalPrelimConfirmation) by the NEMO to their market participants, as this represents the moment at which the information on the market result (typically coinciding with the global final solution) is provided to the market participants and can thus be exploited for trading on the wholesale energy market. ACER is aware that the indication of the disclosure of the global preliminary solution might occur differently in every NEMO, which means that the transaction timestamp reported for SDAC will differ depending on the relevant NEMO. In case the global final solution does not coincide with the global preliminary solution, a lifecycle event will have to be reported to ACER. Price and quantity information for orders and trades Since in SDAC the market time unit (MTU) defining the granularity/intervals for the trading period specifies quarter-hour blocks (i.e. 15-minute MTU), it is expected that the price information for trades resulting from the auction based on the set clearing price reflect the 15-minute granularity. This means that the price of the trade shall be reported by specifying the clearing price in Data Field (87) Price/time interval for each 15-minute MTU (i.e. 15-minute intervals reported in Data Field (84) Load delivery interval) in the priceIntervalQuantityDetails section in the TradeList. This requirement shall be respected irrespective of whether the trade refers to a 15-, 30- or 60-minute product. It is understood that certain auctions markets apply 30-minute granularity/intervals for the trading period (i.e. 30-minute MTU), therefore, in the case of transactions places/concluded in such auctions, the applicable reporting requirements shall follow as described above but applying the 30-minute granularity. The abovementioned requirement is also considered applicable to orders, provided the reported price information always reflects the price of the order. For the quantity information, the same logic shall be considered applicable as for the price (i.e. it shall follow the granularity of the relevant MTU). For the correct reporting of the total notional contract quantity, see the guidance provided under Data Field (54). Load delivery intervals for orders and trades The intervals reported in Data Field (84) Load delivery interval shall always indicate the date and time of the interval for both orders and trades. In addition, the intervals shall always be reported in a chronological order, with each consecutive interval relevant to the order and trade. This means that grouping together several non-consecutive intervals that have the same price and/or quantity is not allowed. In the case of aggregated curves, the price shall determine the order of the intervals in an ascending manner (lowest to highest). The Contract List shall reflect whether the product is a 30-minute or 60-minute product by reporting the deliveryStartDateTime and deliveryEndDateTime, along with the loadDeliveryStartDateTime and loadDeliveryEndDateTime with the delivery interval of the product (i.e. 30- or 60-minute). Lifecycle reporting requirements For the reporting requirements of lifecycle events in relation to transactions placed and concluded on auction markets, see Annex I to the TRUM.

It is ACER’s understanding that in pay-as-bid auctions the transmission system operator (TSO) simultaneously acts as a market participant on the buy side and as an OMP, by facilitating that multiple third-party buying or selling interests in wholesale energy products interact in a manner that may result in a transaction. In the REMIT reporting, in the case of such a pay-as-bid auction, the TSO’s demand side is expected to be reflected in the form of an order report (buy side order), by using Table 1, even though it does not fully reflect the actual market activity in the sense that the TSO’s order was not entered into the order book. In doing so, in the TSO’s order report Data Field (1) ID of the market participant shall identify the relevant TSO with one of the accepted codes registered in the Centralised European Register of Energy Market Participants (CEREMP), and an order ID shall be artificially assigned to the TSO’s (buy) order and reported in Data Field (15) Order ID. The transaction timestamp of the TSO’s (buy) order is expected to be the time of the gate closure. In the case of pay-as-bid auctions, Data Field (25) Contract type shall be populated with value ‘AU_PAB’ for the reported orders and trades linked to the auction.

Market participants may enter into transactions on organised marketplaces by acting on the account of a third-party by the means of direct electronic access (DEA)( ). Hence, in case the transactions placed or concluded under a DEA arrangement are to be reported under REMIT, Table 1 shall be used. While in general it is understood that the reporting requirements described in the TRUM for transactions placed or concluded on an OMP under a DEA arrangement shall not differ from those applicable for any other OMP transaction, it is crucial to correctly identify in the transaction report the parties involved in the ‘DEA chain’. More specifically, the DEA chain always involves the DEA provider (being the exchange member and owner of the trading account) and the DEA client acquiring access to the DEA provider’s account through direct delegation. In addition, in some cases the DEA chain may include sub-delegation. The DEA client or the sub-delegated client(s) may place or conclude the transaction on its own behalf or on behalf of a final beneficiary. While the below sections aim to clarify the general principle and understanding over the role of the different parties involved in the DEA chain and the respective transaction reporting requirements, more detailed guidance on the reporting is available under Data Fields (9), (10) and (12). DEA Provider When the DEA provider offers the DEA service to the DEA client to trade on an OMP, this means that the transactions are placed or concluded by the DEA client via the account of the DEA provider. Since the DEA provider is the registered member of the OMP, it is considered a market participant under REMIT (given that it bears responsibility for the trading activity), hence shall be identified in Data Field

(1) ID of the market participant or counterparty via one of its unique codes registered in CEREMP. This does not necessarily imply that the DEA provider is the decision maker, but it is responsible towards the OMP. DEA client When a DEA client uses the account of the DEA provider for its trading activity, it is understood that the DEA client enters into transactions by acting on the account of the DEA provider ( ). Therefore, in this scenario the DEA client is a market participant under REMIT and must be identified in Data Field (9) ID of the market participants acting on a third-party account via one of its unique codes registered in CEREMP. When using the account of the DEA provider, the DEA client may enter into transactions on its own behalf or on behalf of a final beneficiary. Given that the DEA provider is the registered member of the OMP, and the DEA provider and the DEA client are in a direct contractual relationship, both the DEA provider and its client shall ensure that the DEA client is correctly identified towards the OMP at transaction level in the REMIT reporting. Sub-delegation Depending on the business model established for a given DEA service agreement, the DEA client (client 1) may be allowed by the DEA provider to sub-delegate the DEA provider’s trading account to a sub-delegated client (client 2). Under such a scenario, it is understood that the DEA client (client 1) is in a
( ) For the definition of direct electronic access, see Article 2(19) of REMIT ( ) Note that this scenario refers to the case when there is no sub-delegation in place direct contractual relationship with both the DEA provider and also with the DEA sub-delegated client (client 2), therefore, client 1 is considered as an intermediate beneficiary ( ) towards the DEA provider. In such configuration, the sub-delegated client (Client 2) that is effectively using the DEA provider’s account to trade on the OMP is considered a REMIT market participant given the fact that it is entering into transactions on a wholesale energy market. Hence, it shall be registered with the relevant NRA pursuant to Article 9 of REMIT. The sub-delegated client (client 2) may carry out its trading activity on its own behalf or on behalf of a final beneficiary. Regarding the REMIT reporting requirements in case of sub-delegation, the DEA client (client 1) that is passing further the trading account to client 2 shall always appear in Data Field (9) given that towards the DEA provider client 1 is considered an intermediate beneficiary, as per Article 8(1) of REMIT. In addition to the ID of the DEA client, also the sub-delegated client (client 2), being a market participant when using the account of the DEA provider for placing or concluding the transaction, is to be identified in Data Field (9). It is understood that in certain arrangements, such reporting may not be permittable at a transaction reporting level due to confidentiality restrictions within the DEA chain, nevertheless, the sub-delegated client (client 2) placing or concluding the transaction shall still comply with its registration obligation under Article 9 of REMIT. If the information on the sub-delegated client (client 2) placing or concluding the transaction is known by the OMP either at the time the reporting is due or afterwards, Data Field (9) should be reported, respectively, either in the record with Action type N or as its modification with Action type M, with the corresponding ID of the client (where contractually permitted). Furthermore, at the schema level the applicable <deaSubdelegation> flag (being a mandatory field) shall be populated with value ‘true’ in case of sub-delegation. The information on the sub-delegation is expected to be communicated towards the OMP by the DEA client (client 1) directly, if applicable, or via the DEA provider. Final beneficiary As explained above, the correct representation of the different entities involved in the DEA is essential. In a similar fashion, pursuant to Article 8(1) of REMIT, the correct identification of the final beneficiary is also of key importance in the REMIT transaction reporting. Data Field (10) Beneficiary ID shall identify the final beneficiary of the transaction when the beneficiary is not the same as the market participant identified in Data Field (1) or in Data Field (9). In general, the OMP shall report the final beneficiary information once it is available to the OMP, and this should apply also in case the reportable transaction was placed or concluded under a DEA arrangement. As mentioned above, it might be the case that the sub-delegated client (client 2) carries out the trading activity on its own behalf, but it cannot be identified in Data Field (9) since this information may not be available to the OMP. Nevertheless, the final beneficiary information shall still be reported by the OMP in the record reported with Action type N or, once known, as a modification with Action type M, even if the final beneficiary may be the sub-delegated client (client 2) that was actually trading on its own behalf (hence it should have been identified in Data Field (9)). The ID of the sub-delegated client (client 2) is expected be reported as a modification in Data Field (9) with Action type M once it becomes available to the OMP, if contractually permittable, irrespective of whether the sub-delegated client (client 2) has been identified earlier in the record as a final beneficiary in Data Field (10). Ensuring the identification of the final beneficiary in the transaction report (latest as a lifecycle event) is the responsibility of the market participant trading on behalf of the final beneficiary, if this information is not known by the OMP.
( ) Article 8(1) of REMIT specifies that information reported within a record of wholesale energy market transactions shall include, inter alia, the intermediate or final beneficiaries of the transaction.

units.b: Trading on an exchange with orders placed on a broker platform
units.t: If the trade takes place on an exchange with the related orders placed on a broker-type OMP (i.e. via screen or voice-assisted), the resulting trade should be reported as any other trade that takes place on an exchange. If traded on the broker’s screen, the orders should be reported to reflect that the orders were placed on a contract advertised by the exchange. There is no expectation that the order report and the trade report are linked together as they were placed first and executed later on two different OMPs. When orders on futures traded on exchanges are placed on the broker platforms, for example indication of interest (IOI), Data Field (6) ID of the other market participant (counterparty) should include the ID of the exchange. This can be reported in the form of the legal entity identifier (LEI), bank identifier code (BIC), energy identification code (EIC), ACER code or market identifier code (MIC) code.

It is ACER’s understanding that a Click & Trade order is a limit order which aggresses the initiator order. In the case of Click & Trade, ACER shall receive two trade reports (buy and sell side) and only one order report in the event that the trade fully extinguishes the initiating order. The initiator shall report an order and a trade populating Data Field (14) with ‘I’ for ‘Initiator’ and Data Field (16) Order type with ‘LIM’, while the aggressor aggressing the initiator’s order shall report the trade by populating the tag ‘clickAndTradeDetails’ in the Trade List of the electronic format with the information on the order of the initiator. It is understood that the conclusion of the trade takes place on the OMP, therefore, the order record and the resulted trade records (for the two sides) are expected to be reported by the OMP. It may happen that some trading systems automatically create the order for the aggressor when a Click & Trade takes place. In this case, when reporting Click & Trade transactions, the reporting party can decide to also report the aggressor’s order.

With reference to the clearing (or registration) of a trade concluded bilaterally or on a broker-type OMP, the cleared/registered trade shall be reported to ACER by the clearing exchange OMP indicating the following information in the trade report.
• Data Field (33) Organised marketplace ID/OTC shall be populated with the unique code of the exchange where the trade is cleared/registered.
• In addition, the exchange is expected to flag whether the original trade (agreement) which was subsequently sent for clearing was concluded on a broker-type OMP or bilaterally. This means that the registered identification code of broker-type OMP or value ‘XBIL’ respectively shall be populated in the dedicated schema field <sourceOMPID> in the Trade List.
• Data Field (37) Transaction timestamp shall indicate the timestamp of the clearing/trade registration.
• Data Field (40) Linked order ID shall be reported with the default value ‘NA’.
• Data Field (43) Transaction type shall be populated with ‘CL’ for ‘Cleared’ in order to flag the cleared trade.
• There is no requirement that the original trade (that was agreed bilaterally or concluded on a broker-type OMP) and the cleared trade reports are linked together in the REMIT reporting, however, reporting parties may establish such linkage in their reporting. If the original trade that was subsequently sent for clearing (trade registration) was concluded on a broker-type OMP, the related orders and the resulting trade (including their lifecycle events taking place on the OMP) are considered reportable by the broker-type OMP. It is important to note that when the clearing occurs, the original transactions reported shall not be cancelled with Action type C as a lifecycle event.
If the trade was originally agreed bilaterally, it is expected to be reported as a bilateral trade by the relevant market participants as the counterparties, provided the bilateral trade represents a firm trade at the time of the agreement. In case the bilateral trade becomes firm only upon clearing/trade registration, the original bilateral agreement is not considered a reportable transaction. It may also happen that the trade registered by the exchange for clearing refers to two separate trades concluded by the same counterparties on the broker-type OMPs. For example: 1. trade 1: on 15 August, market participant A executes on a broker platform a transaction with market participant B for a volume V1 and price P1;
2. trade 2: on 17 August, the same market participants execute another transaction on a broker platform for a volume V2 and price P2;
3. trade 3: on 20 August, market participant A registers at the exchange for clearing purpose an OTC transaction with market participant B for volume V = V1 + V2 and at a price of P (potentially different from P1 or P2).
In such a scenario, Trade 1 and Trade 2 are expected to be reported by the broker-type OMP by indicating the ID of the broker-type OMP in Data Field (33), by reporting the respective price and quantity information and being assigned with different UTIs. On the other hand, Trade 3 is expected to be reported by the exchange OMP that has registered the trade by reporting volume V and price P in the trade reporting (together with the information the clearing exchange is required to report as described above).

In the context of transaction reporting, the following scenario and reporting requirements are to be considered regarding local flexibility products. Scenario: the exchange decides to offer the possibility to trade local flexibility products. The platform offered by the exchange is used by, on the buy side, the TSO / distribution system operator (via the system operator) to access the liquidity of the exchange to coordinate their congestion management solutions, and, on the sell side, the exchange members. Despite the presence of an aggregator (i.e. the system operator) with the function of reducing congestion in the electricity grid, this arrangement represents the bringing together of multiple third-party buying and selling interests in wholesale energy products in a way that results in a contract. Therefore, such contracts are considered as standard contracts traded on an OMP, having both the orders and trades to be reported by using Table 1. When reporting the transactions in Table 1, the following requirements shall be met.
• Both Data Field (23) Contract ID and Data Field (24) Contract name shall start with the prefix ‘CM_’, followed by the contract ID and contract name, respectively, assigned by the OMP. The prefix ‘CM’ shall stand for ‘Congestion Management’.
• Data Field (33) Organised marketplace ID/OTC shall identify the OMP on which the order was placed, and the trade was concluded related to the local flexibility product.
• Data Field (78) Delivery point or zone shall be populated with the EIC of the relevant balancing zone or market area for delivery, and the relevant EAN code to indicate the locational information via the unique identification number that links the respective connection point to a specific user/address.

It is understood that within-day contracts for the supply of natural gas feature a delivery time covering the remainder of the current gas delivery day at the time the trade is concluded. In ACER’s understanding there are some European countries where gas within-day contracts can be delivered from 06:00 am to 06:00 am of the following day (daily balancing), while in other European countries there are 24 tradable contracts, one for each hour from 06:00 am to 06:00 am of the following day (hourly balancing). When a within-day contract features daily balancing in its contract specification, the relevant order and trade records are expected to refer to 06:00 am to 06:00 am of the following day in the delivery profile in their contract details, while the load delivery intervals in the priceIntervalQuantityDetails section shall be populated with the actual hours of delivery (i.e. the remaining hours until the end of the gas day). It is expected that the order and the related trade record refer to the same contract ID reported in Data Field (23). For further information, see Example 2.20 in Annex II to the TRUM. On the other hand, if the within-day contract traded on an exchange encompasses hourly contracts (hourly balancing), each contract shall be assigned with a different contract ID. In this case, the applied reporting logic is the same as for most of the hourly electricity contracts represented in Annex II to the TRUM. However, in some circumstances, for example when gas within-day contracts are traded on broker platforms and are related to markets with hourly balancing, this may be handled differently.

In ACER’s understanding, the typical structure of non-standard contracts for the supply or storage of electricity or the supply of natural gas may include:
• general or master agreement (‘main body’);
• election sheet;
• annexes (part of the general agreement by default); and
• individual transactions (constituting the economic terms) precisely defining the energy-related contract. Master agreements typically serve the purpose of setting out the rules for trading activities of the two counterparties of a contract, but do not set any obligation on the two parties. The conclusion of such a general agreement (e.g. general agreement for the delivery and acceptance of electricity) setting out the general terms for trading without specifying the price setting of volume optionality, for example, the amount of electricity, time and place of delivery and price, is not a reportable contract under REMIT. However, the individual contracts concluded under the terms of a general agreement concerning the delivery and acceptance of electricity shall be reported.
Other master agreements may not include some of the parts indicated above but are general contracts for the supply of electricity or natural gas that have two main parts: a commercial part and an economic part. If market participants have agreed on the commercial terms under a general agreement, they may:
1. negotiate the economic terms and conclude a trade (commercial and economic terms), which will result in a bilateral trade reportable in Table 1; or
2. negotiate the economic terms and conclude a contract (commercial and economic terms) with flexibility, which will result in a non-standard contract reportable in Table 2 (price and quantity may change at a later stage).
Alternatively, depending on the agreement, market participants may have already agreed the commercial and economic terms in one agreement (contract) which includes non-standard contract clauses, such as take or pay and/or reselling of already purchased quantities and/or different pre-defined pricing formulas. Under such a contract, which is considered a REMIT non-standard contract reportable in Table 2, the following features apply:
• quantities are not necessarily pre-defined;
• the price is pre-defined (e.g. by formula or index) but may not be fixed; and
• at least one of the market participants is obliged to deliver/offtake agreed quantity or has the single right to request this from the other market participant.
Under this type of agreement there may be different nomination, pricing flexibility, option exercise and possibility to enter into forward contracts or additional volumes.
Under such a Table 2 non-standard contract, market participants may do the following.
1. Negotiate the economic terms and conclude a trade considered as bilateral trade reportable in Table 1 under REMIT. In such a case, the contract name reported in Data Field (24) shall be populated with the default value ‘BILCONTRACT’ and Data Field (39) Linked Transaction ID shall include the contract ID of the non-standard contract reported in Table 2.
Or 2. Conclude executions under the framework of the non-standard contract using the flexibility and fixing events, considered as executions reported in Table 1 under REMIT. In such a case, the contract name reported in Data Field (24) shall be populated with the default value ‘EXECUTION’ and Data Field (39) Linked Transaction ID shall include the contract ID of the non-standard contract reported in Table 2. Each execution report shall be assigned with a unique transaction identification in Data Field (38) Unique Transaction ID of Table 1.
Executions

In the context of REMIT transaction reporting, execution shall be understood as executed deliveries concluded under a non-standard contract previously reported in Table 2. Executions shall be reported in Table 1 when the outright price and quantity of the execution are available and are linked to the relevant non-standard contract (hence they may also be called ‘invoiced’ executions).
In the case of executions, ACER understands that once the volume and the price of the transaction is known to the counterparties, the transaction is complete. This can occur after the delivery of the commodity. In the context of executions, each exercise of the contractual right to deliver the agreed energy in an EU delivery point or zone is a reportable transaction. When reporting executions, the relevant delivery point or zone shall be identified in Data Field (78) according to ACER’s list of accepted EICs available on the REMIT Portal.
It is important to note some nuances between a physical spot/forward contract traded on an OMP with a price settled against an index and an execution under the framework of a non-standard contract which settles days after the delivery of the energy commodity ends. In fact, both two transactions may not have a fixed price or volume before the delivery of the energy commodity starts and, most likely, both of them will be completely settled after the delivery period ends. However, while the physical spot/forward contract traded on an OMP is reported with the contracted volume and the fixing index (which most likely is publicly available), the transaction executed under the framework of a non-standard contract has to be reported once the delivered quantity and the price are known. Therefore, the date and time of the two execution records reported by the counterparties may be different.
ACER understands that the details of transactions executed within the framework of non-standard contracts are available to both parties to the contract by the invoicing date at the latest. On that basis, executions under the framework of non-standard contracts are reportable no later than 10 working days after the invoicing date at the latest. In ACER’s understanding this implies that the billing cycle and invoicing date is the last point in time when the price and quantity can be discovered. However, in the context of the billing cycle and the invoicing date, the different components of the invoice, such as taxes, costs and different adjustments, are not in the scope of REMIT. Market participants shall report the energy price for the energy delivered in the period the reported execution refers to.
Market participants reporting transactions executed within the framework of non-standard contracts should report the energy price as considered in the contract. If the price is fixed, that outright price is expected to be reported. If the price is fixed by a fixing index, a price formula defined in the contract or a strike price in the case of option contracts, then that energy price must be reported in the execution report. Regarding the energy delivered, market participants shall report the energy delivered as indicated in the execution report.

ACER understands that invoices may cover several months: the current month plus some adjustments from previous months (these can sometimes go back up to several months in the past). Market participants have to report only the energy delivered in the period the execution report refers to without any adjustments from the past. If the reporting of the energy delivered in the previous month is overestimated or underestimated, nothing would prevent market participants updating the previously reported execution report with Action type M as lifecycle. When executions under the framework of a non-standard contract have a price which is set with different price formulas depending on the delivery point of the commodity, then these executions should be reported separately (one report for each delivery point). If the price is set with one price formula for all the delivery points of the commodity, and the volume split is known to the market participant, then these executions should be reported separately (one report for each delivery point). If the volume split is not known to the market participant, then these executions can be reported with one report (e.g. one report indicating the total volume and indicating, for example, two delivery points).
It is also important to note that within the framework of a non-standard contract, for those periods when there is no delivery, there is no need to report executions. In addition, where the framework of a non-standard contract allows for the sale and purchase of energy under the same contract, market participants shall not net those executions, as in some circumstances they may lead to zero volume at the end of the month. Market participants need to report the sold and bought volumes separately with different execution reports in Table 1.
ACER understands that there are contracts with a joint venture of producers of certain fields. In the case of such joint ventures there are separate contracts with each of the parties participating in that field, but that invoicing is done with only one partner, often referred to as ‘the operator’ of the field. In such cases, in the context of reporting the executions, those contracts should be reported separately, allocating the delivered volume to the respective contracts (counterparties) and reporting as many transactions as the number of counterparties to contracts related to the same gas field.

Portfolio-type contracts concluded between the counterparties for the delivery of LNG shall not be considered the same as the general/master agreements described in Section 2.2.1. Portfolio-type contracts are defined as short-, mid- or long-term binding agreements between the counterparties, typically including:
• pre-defined pricing formulas (typically expressed as complex price formula);
• pre-defined (but not necessarily fully fixed) quantities or number of cargos to be delivered under the portfolio; and/or
• other flexibility and optionality clauses. Under portfolio-type contracts, the counterparties subsequently agree on cargo nominations to fulfil their delivery obligation, which will result in the execution/individual delivery of the cargo(s) at the agreed LNG terminal. Given the different flexibilities and optionalities that portfolio-type contracts typically include, they are considered non-standard contracts to be reported in Table 2 under the REMIT transaction reporting framework but are not considered reportable as LNG market data. Cargo nominations under portfolio-type contracts specifying the delivery of LNG in the EU are, however, considered reportable as LNG market data in the dedicated REMITTable1LNG schema, therefore Annex III to the TRUM on reporting LNG market and trade data shall be consulted. The LNG market data for cargo nominations reported in the REMITTable1LNG schema shall always provide the contract ID of the related non-standard contract previously reported in Table 2. In case the LNG market data record on cargo nomination is reported earlier than the first Table 2 record with Action type N for the portfolio-type contract (this may happen given the different reporting timelines), the contract ID of the portfolio-type contract may need to be reported as a lifecycle event to the LNG market data record. LNG supply contracts can be concluded based on two distinct delivery terms, i.e. on DES (delivery-ex-ship) or FOB (free-on-board) basis. Therefore, the delivery terms of the LNG portfolio-type contract reported in Table 2 shall always be specified in Data Field (18) Delivery terms. If the portfolio-type contract does not specify any (fixed or potential) EU delivery, the contract is not reportable under REMIT at the time of the agreement. If there is a later decision to deliver LNG in the EU, the portfolio-type contract becomes reportable in Table 2 in T + 10 working days from the day the delivery into the EU was agreed by indicating the terms and conditions of the contract relevant for EU deliveries. The Table 2 report shall indicate the EIC code of the agreed EU delivery terminal, but the economic terms shall reflect the optionality and flexibilities included in the original contract. It is important to note that the actual cargo nominations are reportable in real time as LNG market data upon the agreement on the delivery. In case the portfolio-type contract (with volume, price and/or delivery window optionality) specifies EU delivery but without the actual EU LNG terminal(s) where the delivery shall happen, it is to be reported as a non-standard contract in Table 2 by indicating the delivery point with EIC 21W000000ACELNGX, which represents all LNG terminals located in the EU. Later when the specific EU LNG terminal where the cargo shall arrive is agreed between the counterparties, the agreement becomes reportable as LNG market data related to the cargo nomination and it shall indicate the EIC of the actual LNG terminal where the cargo delivery will take place. If the portfolio-type contract specifies the optionality to deliver the commodity at more than one EU LNG terminal or/and other terminals outside the EU, the LNG market participant shall report the contract in Table 2 by including all the EIC W codes related to EU LNG terminals in the report. The agreed cargo nominations are reportable as LNG market data. Market participants are expected to consult Annex II to the TRUM on examples for reporting LNG portfolio-type non-standard contracts using Table 2, and Annex I to the TRUM for the lifecycle reporting requirements applicable to non-standard contracts. For further information on the reporting requirements for LNG market data, see Chapter 5 of the TRUM and also Annex III to the TRUM, in particular.

units.b: Delivery point or zone for supply contracts
units.t: The accurate identification of the delivery point or zone of the supply contract in the reported transaction report is a fundamental requirement in the transaction reporting guidance under REMIT and is mandatory information for all transactions reported in Table 1 and Table 2 in Data Field (78) and Data Field (46) respectively. These fields shall indicate the EIC Y, Z or W code to identify the delivery point or zone for the contract. Any contract related to the supply of electricity or natural gas, irrespective of whether it is a spot, a physical forward, a future or an option contract, has a reference to a delivery point or zone. Also, financial derivatives related to EU electricity or gas have a reference price or other attributes that relate to the delivery of the commodity. ACER publishes and updates on a regular basis the list of accepted EICs for REMIT transaction reporting purposes on the ACER website. The transaction reports reported with an EIC in Data Field

units.b: Delivery point or zone for supply contracts
units.t:
(78) and (46) in Table 1 and Table 2 respectively that is not included in the list will be rejected by the relevant validation rule. Additional codes that represent delivery points for REMIT transaction reporting purposes not currently listed should be conveyed to the online EICs Reporting Form.
Electricity delivery point or zone The delivery point or zone of a contract for the supply of electricity can be of two types. 1. Balancing zone. This is the zone for which the system operator is responsible for keeping the electricity in balance. Market participants will deliver and take the delivery (transfer of ownership of the commodity) of the electricity through their nominations, for example, the notification of the electricity delivered or withdrawn into or from the system to the system operator. 2. Market area. This is the area that the specific contract refers to. It can be the same as the balancing area, or it can encompass several balancing areas. Gas delivery point or zone The delivery point or zone of a contract for the supply of gas can be of four types. 1. Balancing zone. This is the zone for which the system operator is responsible for keeping the gas in balance. Market participants will deliver and take the delivery (transfer of ownership of the commodity) of the gas through their nominations, for example, the notification of the gas delivered or withdrawn into or from the system to the system operator. 2. Market area. This is the area that the specific contract refers to. It can be the same as the balancing area, or it can encompass several balancing areas. 3. Interconnection or entry point. These points can be defined as follows. a. The interconnection point is the point where gas is delivered and then transferred to the other side of the interconnection point by the system operator. This case applies to unbundled interconnection capacity only. For example, interconnection between area (A), managed by system operator (TSO_X), and area (B), managed by the neighbouring system operator (TSO_Y), which can be explained as follows. i. Market participant (MP1) delivers and balances its position at point (A) with TSO_X. Market participant (MP1) makes its nomination at point (A) with TSO_X. ii. The system operators TSO_X and TSO_Y transfer the energy from point (A) to point (B). iii. Market participant (MP2) delivers the gas and balances its position at point (B) with TSO_Y while the market participant (MP2) makes the nomination at point (B). iv. Delivery at interconnection points across two EU Member States must be reported only in the case of unbundled capacity. In all other cases the balancing zone or market area should be reported (see point 3(a)) above. v. Delivery at interconnection points across a non-EU country and an EU Member State with unbundled capacity must be reported only in case of flow in the direction of the Member State. For example, two counterparties have a gas contract for the delivery at interconnection points with unbundled capacity (also called at the border). If the gas flows from the non-EU country to the EU Member State, the contract is reportable under REMIT as the counterparty (in the contract) receiving the gas is registered in the Member State. On the contrary if the gas flows from the EU to the non-EU country, the contract is not reportable under REMIT as the counterparty receiving the gas is based in a non-EU country. b. The entry point (e.g. terminal) is the physical delivery point where the commodity changes hands at an entry point. For example, this can be a terminal (e.g. Eemshaven) in the Netherlands where a seller delivers the gas to the buyer before the gas flows into the TTF hub (balancing zone). 4. Natural gas storage or LNG facility. This is the gas facility the contract refers to (physical location). The delivery point should be reported in line with what is specified in the contract. If the contract refers to a specific sub-terminal, then both parties should report the corresponding EIC code for that sub-terminal. If the contract instead refers to the main terminal, the EIC W code for the aggregate terminal may be used.

units.b: Supply contracts to be reported on a periodic basis
Transportation contracts to be reported on a continuous basis
Continuous explicit intraday cross-border capacity allocation
units.t: In case when the relevant allocation rules define that the allocated intraday cross-border capacity is automatically nominated with no possibility of intervention from the market participant and that the amounts of allocated and nominated intraday cross-border capacity are equal, then there is no need for the relevant TSOs or third party acting on their behalf to submit separate reports for both the allocated and nominated capacity information. Only the nominated cross-border capacity shall be reported to ACER. In case the relevant allocation rules allow the market participant to nominate a different amount of cross-border capacity to the allocated amount, then both the allocated and the nominated capacity will have to be reported to ACER.

units.b: Capacity conversion from unbundled to bundled capacity
units.t:
In the case of capacity conversion from unbundled to bundled capacity, the initial capacity contract needs to be modified after the conversion by indicating the following information in the modified report.
Scenario 1. The capacity conversion applies to the entire period of the initial capacity contract:
• Data Field (5) Transportation transaction identification shall be populated with the same transaction ID as the initial capacity contract;
• Data Field (18) Action type shall be populated with ‘66G’ for ‘Changed’;
• Data Field (19) Quantity shall indicate ‘0’ (zero) quantity to flag that all the capacity has been converted into bundled capacity;
• Data Field (27) Bundling shall indicate ‘ZEP’ for ‘Unbundled capacity’.
Scenario 2. The capacity conversion applies only to a certain part(s) of the total period included in the initial capacity contract. In this case, both periods – where the capacity conversion applies and where it does not – shall be reported in the same file (i.e. in the modified report) and shall be indicated in the following way.

In both scenarios, since capacity conversion constitutes a change in the main contractual aspects (product quality), TSOs will also have to report the transformation of the initial capacity contract as a new contract, by indicating the following information in the new report:
• Data Field (5) Transportation transaction identification shall be populated with a new transaction ID compared to that of the initial capacity contract;
• Data Field (13) Start date and time and Data Field (14) End date and time shall indicate only the period(s) for which the capacity conversion is applied;
• Data Field (18) Action type shall be populated with ‘62G’ for ‘Active’;
• Data Field (27) Bundling shall indicate ‘ZEO’ for ‘Bundled capacity’.
In the case of bundled capacity, each reporting party reports its contractual part of the transaction.

units.b: Capacity upgrade from interruptible to firm capacity
units.t: The same approach as described above for capacity conversion is expected to be applied when the capacity underlying the initial capacity contract has been upgraded from interruptible to firm capacity. In this case, Data Field (16) Capacity category shall be populated with ‘Z05’ for ‘interruptible (booked)’ in the modified report of the initial capacity contract. For the new contract which results from the capacity upgrade, Data Field (16) shall be populated with the code of the relevant capacity type/category, for example, ZEQ, Z06, ZES, ZET, etc.

In the case of floating tariffs, the regulated price, i.e. capacity charges, are not fixed. In the case of long-term contracts, it is understood that there is no need to send tariff changes as a modification of the contract if the usage of the tariff is well-defined in a contract and if the tariff change is made publicly available by the TSO or by the respective NRA.

In relation to contracts for supply, as set out to Article 7c of REMIT, LNG market participants shall submit daily to ACER the LNG market data, free of charge, by means of the reporting channels established by ACER, in a standardised format, through a high-quality transmission protocol, and as close to real-time as technologically possible before the publication of the daily LNG price assessment (18:00 CET).
In addition, contracts for the supply of LNG with delivery in the EU are considered reportable under REMIT as set out in Article 3(a) of the REMIT Implementing Regulation.
In order to allow the streamlined reporting of transactions that fall under the scope of both reporting obligations mentioned above (referred to as ‘LNG market and trade data’), such transactions shall be reported by using the dedicated electronic format, i.e. Table1LNG.
The dedicated guidance on how to report LNG market and trade data under REMIT is available in Annex III to the TRUM.

units.b: Data Field (1) ID of the market participant
units.t:
ID of the market participant
<idOfMarketParticipant>
ACER code Alphanumerical 12 A0643278W.EU LEI 20 1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8e9f0h BIC 11 ACERSILJ500 EIC 16 21X000EUROPEU–8 GLN / GS1 code 13 a1b2c3d4e5f6g
This field shall identify the market participant placing or concluding the transaction by its unique identification code on whose behalf the transaction is reported. In addition, for the purpose of the REMIT reporting and in the context of concluded trades, the other market participant that is the actual counterparty to the market participant identified in Data Field (1) is referred to as the other market participant being identified in Data Field (6). The market participant that places the order or concludes the trade has to be identified in the transaction report as the responsible entity for the trading activity. This does not necessarily imply that this market participant is the actual counterparty or the final beneficiary to the transaction, but it is responsible for the reporting. For example, in case of a DEA arrangement, the DEA provider shall be identified in this field (for further guidance, see Section 132.1.2.1). The ID of the market participant identified in Data Field (1) is considered part of the unique key of the transaction record, it shall therefore remain unique throughout the lifecycle of the transaction. For more information, see Annex I to the TRUM. The field is mandatory for all transactions reported in Table 1. ACER code of the market participant The market participant shall be identified in Data Field (1) by one of the unique codes registered with its NRA and available in CEREMP. If the market participant possesses different types of unique identification codes listed as accepted values under this field, all these need to be provided to the NRA, and thus be made available in CEREMP, upon the registration of the market participant. When the market participant registers with the relevant NRA, the market participant will receive an ACER code. From ACER’s perspective, it is preferable to use the ACER code from the reporting point of view. Nevertheless, for example, if a market participant is already using the LEI code for European Market Infrastructure Regulation ( ) (EMIR) reporting, that market participant may also use the LEI
( ) Regulation (EU) No 648/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on OTC derivatives, central counterparties and trade repositories (OJ L 201, 27.7.2012, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2012/648/oj). code for REMIT reporting, as long as the LEI code has been provided to the relevant NRA in the registration process. If a market participant is using its ACER code, this can be used by its counterparty to verify the identity of the market participant through CEREMP available on the REMIT Portal. It may occur that the ACER code is not known to the OMP or to the other reporting party reporting on behalf of the market participant. If the ACER code has not been provided by the market participant to the OMP (for OMP transactions) or to the other reporting party reporting on behalf of the market participant (for bilateral trades), one of the alternative codes listed above and registered in CEREMP shall be used; otherwise, the report will be rejected as invalid.

units.b: Data Field (2) Type of code used in field 1
units.t:
Type of code used in field 1
ACER code Text 3 ace LEI 3 lei BIC 3 bic EIC 3 eic GLN/GS1 code 3 gln
This field identifies the type of code used in Data Field (1). For example, if a LEI code is used in the report to identify the market participant in Data Field (1), the accepted value in this field shall be ‘lei’. If an ACER code is used in Data Field (1), the accepted value reported in this field is ‘ace’. If a market participant which is a financial entity chooses to use a BIC code for Data Field (1), it could be the case that the code is less than 11 characters long. In such a case, typically when an 8-digit code is given, the code has to be reported by adding ‘XXX’ at the end, to ensure the 11-digit length. The field is mandatory for all transactions reported in Table 1.

Liquidity provision activity
<liquidityProviderIndicator>
true Text 5 true false The field shall identify whether the market participant reported in Data Field (1) has placed the reportable order on the OMP as part of a contractual arrangement with the OMP for providing a service for market making. In such case, in the order report this field shall be populated with ‘true’. The liquidity provider (market maker) is considered a member of the OMP. Nevertheless, ACER acknowledges that under the financial regulation in some specific cases such a function could also be carried out by the client of the member (e.g. DEA client) using the member’s account for the trading activity. If by placing the order the market participant provides liquidity under its normal business operation (not under a formal liquidity provision agreement with the OMP), the value ‘false’ shall be reported. The flag under this field is expected to be populated by the OMP when reporting its order book given that the flag is intended to identify such orders that have been placed as per the market marking service agreement in place with the OMP. In case the OMP already has arrangements in place in its trading system to flag activities related to liquidity provision activities as per its obligation under the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID) ( ), the OMP may apply the same reporting logic and process for transactions related to liquidity provision activities as established under its MiFID reporting. The field is mandatory only for orders to trades.

units.b: Data Field (4) ID of the trader
units.t:
ID of the trader
<traderID>
Up to 100 alphanumerical digits Alphanumeric 100 1234567890abcdefghi
Field description and cardinality This field indicates the ID used by the OMP or by the market participant to identify the user responsible for entering into a transaction that is to be reported. In ACER’s understanding this is typically an electronic ID for the trader’s account or a technical representation of that account. As the same trader may have multiple IDs, it is crucial that the relevant ID used by the trader for that particular transaction that is to be reported is always provided in this field. This field is considered mandatory in the sense that there must be an identifier of the person or group of people responsible for taking decisions or actions in executing or amending the transaction. A number
( ) Directive 2004/39/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 April 2004 on markets in financial instruments amending Council Directives 85/611/EEC and 93/6/EEC and Directive 2000/12/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 93/22/EEC (OJ L 145, 30.4.2004, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/39/oj). or code does not disclose the identity of the person in the transaction reporting; thus, market participants and OMPs may report a number (or code) to avoid the reporting of names. It is ACER’s understanding that even if an algorithm is being used for the placing or the conclusion of the transaction, there is a ‘human’ trader responsible for the application of the algorithm for that particular transaction. Therefore, this field is considered mandatory irrespective of whether the placing or conclusion of the transaction involved algorithmic trading or not. The field is mandatory for all orders and trades placed/concluded on an OMP or bilaterally, except for executions. OMP transactions In the case of transactions placed or concluded on an OMP, this field shall represent how the OMP identifies the trader. The uniqueness of the trader ID shall be maintained even if the trader is responsible for multiple algorithms. With regard to orders to trade placed by executing brokers at the OMP, the trader ID of the executing broker as assigned by the OMP shall be reported in this field, if available to the OMP. Bilateral trades In the case of bilateral trades, this field is expected to represent the person or group of people concluding the trade. This implies that the trader ID is to be populated from the perspective of the market participant. If the trader ID becomes available to the designated reporting entity at a later stage (i.e. after the REMIT reporting of the trade), it is expected to be provided as a modification (update) to the original trade with Action type M.
Example: reporting of the trader ID for OMP and bilateral trades
• The OMP identifies Joe Bloggs with ID = 123Abc.
• The OMP identifies company (A) with ID = CompA123.
• Company (A) identifies Joe Bloggs internally with ID = Abc12345.
Scenario 1 – OMP transactions
• A trader called Joe Bloggs working at company (A) trades on an OMP.
• When the OMP reports the transactions placed/executed by Joe Blogges, the trader ID ‘123Abc’ shall be reported in field 3 as identified by the OMP.
Scenario 2 – bilateral trades
• A trader called Joe Bloggs working at company (A) trades bilaterally.
• The trader ID as identified by company (A) shall be reported in field 3: ‘Abc12345'.

Algorithm ID
<algoId>
Up to 100 alphanumerical digits Alphanumeric 100 1234567890abcdefghi
The field shall identify the ID of the algorithm placing the order and/or executing the trade on the OMP. The field is mandatory in case the trading activity related to the transaction to be reported involved algorithmic trading as defined in Article 2(18) of REMIT and further clarified in the ACER Guidance on REMIT ( ). If the transaction involved only human intervention, the field is not applicable. It is important to note that Data Field (4) ID of the trader is also considered mandatory in the case of algorithmic trading as it is understood that there is always a human trader/user responsible for the conclusion of the transaction. The field is not considered applicable in the case of transactions placed or concluded on auction markets. Algorithms in scope In ACER’s view the guidance on reporting transactions under REMIT that involve algorithmic trading shall be in line with the definition and scope of algorithmic trading as clarified in the ACER Guidance on REMIT in relation to the notification obligation of market participants engaging in algorithmic trading ( ). Therefore, market participants and OMPs are expected to consult the related section of the ACER Guidance on REMIT to comply with the transaction reporting requirements. Identification of the algorithm The identification code of the algorithm is expected to uniquely identify the algorithm used for the reported transaction within the firm, i.e. the market participant in the case of internal (i.e. the market participant’s) or stand-alone vendor algorithms, or the OMP in the case of external (i.e. OMP’s) execution algorithms. This implies that the same ID shall not be shared by multiple algorithms within the same firm. Market participants shall ensure that the algorithms used for their trading activities related to transactions reported under REMIT are available to the relevant OMP. This requirement is particularly relevant in case the market participant is using internal or third-party vendor algorithms (i.e. not the OMP’s execution algorithms). It is understood that when market participants are using in-house or third-party vendor algorithms when trading on an OMP, the algorithm IDs may be required to be registered at the relevant OMP before the algorithm is used for trading on that OMP. In the absence of such registration requirements, the market participants are expected to share the IDs of the applied algorithms with the relevant OMP prior to the REMIT reporting of the transaction.
( ) Chapter 7.2 in ACER Guidance on REMIT (6.1st edition). ( ) See Chapter 7 of the ACER Guidance on REMIT on the application of the obligation on the notification of algorithmic trading and direct electronic access. The abovementioned requirement is meant to ensure that the algorithm ID can be provided in the first lifecycle event of the order/trade record reported with Action type N and maintained consistently throughout the lifecycle of the order. It is essential to note that the identification code of the applied algorithm reported in this data field shall reflect exactly the same algorithm ID as originally assigned by the market participant (in the case of internal or stand-alone vendor algorithms), or by the OMP (in the case of external execution algorithms). The lifecycle reporting requirements related to the information on the algorithm ID is specified in Annex I to the TRUM.

units.b: Data Field (6) ID of the other market participant (counterparty)
units.t:
ID of the other market participant (counterparty)
<otherMarketParticipant>
ACER code Alphanumeric 12 A0643278W.EU LEI 20 1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8e9f0h BIC 11 ACERSILJ500 EIC 16 21X000EUROPEU–8 GLN/GS1 code 13 a1b2c3d4e5f6
This field indicates the ID of the other market participant (counterparty) to the trade that is reported. For bilateral trades and executions, the field is always considered mandatory. The field is not considered applicable to orders to trade. OMP transactions If the trade takes place on an exchange and the other market participant is a central counterparty (CCP), clearing house or a clearing member, this field is not applicable. Exchange-traded contracts are typically traded anonymously, so that neither party to the trade knows the identity of the counterparty. If the trade takes place on an exchange with orders to trade placed on the broker OMP, this trade should be reported as any other trade that takes place on exchange, i.e. Data Field (6) is not applicable. Trade with a market participant without an ACER code When a REMIT market participant enters into a bilateral trade (e.g. a financial swap related to gas delivered in the EU) with a non-REMIT market participant (e.g. a firm that only trades bilateral financial products related to EU gas or electricity and fulfils its reporting obligation under EMIR and never enters into a physical trade), or with a REMIT market participant without an ACER code (e.g. market participant is under registration), it may need to populate Data Field (6) with the fictitious ACER code ‘ACERNONMP.EU’ to indicate that the counterparty to the trade does not have an ACER code. There may be a case where market participant A reports a trade with market participant B which is identified by ‘ACERNONMP.EU’ in the trade report reported by market participant A. Later market participant B registers with its relevant NRA and receives an ACER code. In such a scenario, this would be the case of novation as specified in Annex I to the TRUM.

units.b: Data Field (9) ID of the market participants acting on a third-party account
units.t:
ID of the market participants acting on a third- party account
<clientIdentification>
<clientSequence>
<deaSubdelegation>
Description of accepted values | Type | L | ength | Examples
ACER code Alphanumeric 12 A0643278W.EU LEI 20 1a2b3c4d5e6f7g8e9f0h BIC 11 ACERSILJ500 EIC 16 21X000EUROPEU–8 GLN/GS1 code 13 a1b2c3d4e5f6
The field identifies the market participant placing or concluding a transaction on the account of a third-party, i.e. the account of the market participant identified in Data Field (1). The field is mandatory for transactions taking place on the on the organised marketplace where the account of the market participant identified in Data Field (1) is delegated to another market participant that places or concludes the transactions on the organised marketplace. Direct electronic access As described in Chapter 2.1.2.1 when a DEA provider offers the DEA service to its DEA client (client 1) on an OMP, the transactions are concluded by the DEA client via the account of the DEA provider. This implies that the DEA client shall be identified in this field by one of its unique codes registered in CEREMP, while the DEA provider is to be identified in Data Field (1) (being the registered member of the OMP) via one of its unique codes registered in CEREMP. If the DEA client cannot be identified in the original record with Action type N, the record shall be updated with the ID of the DEA client by using Action type M once available. It is also understood that the DEA client may sub-delegate the trading account of the DEA provider to a sub-delegated client (client 2), if such sub-delegation is allowed by the DEA provider. Such sub-delegation may happen multiple times across the DEA chain in a cascading manner. In the electronic format Data Field (9) is being represented via three schema fields in the client section (being repeatable) in the OrderList and TradeList:
• <clientIdentification>
• <clientSequence>
• <deaSubdelegation> Fields <clientIdentification> and <clientSequence> shall always be populated in case of a DEA to identify the DEA client (client 1). In this case the client sequence number shall always be populated with value ‘1’ together with the unique code of the client as described above. In addition, in case of sub-delegation, the sub-delegated client (e.g. client 2) that is effectively using the account of the DEA provider to place or conclude the reportable transaction is also expected to be reported in field <clientIdentification>, with sequence number populated with value ‘2’. Furthermore, the mandatory field <deaSubdelegation> shall always be reported in order to flag whether for that particular transaction, the DEA client identified with sequence number 1 (client 1) has sub-delegated the account to another client (e.g. identified with sequence number 2), or if client 1 was using the account. In case of sub-delegation, value ‘true’ is to be reported irrespective of the availability of the identification code of the sub-delegated client. Otherwise, value ‘false’ shall be populated. For the reporting of the final beneficiary in case of DEA, see Chapter 2.1.2.1 and Data Field (10).
